summary: A landlocked country in central South America, one of the few countries in the Americas where an indigenous language (Guaraní) is co-official with Spanish and spoken by the majority.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The Spanish founded Asunción in 1537, and Franciscan and Jesuit missionaries followed. From 1609 the Jesuits established dozens of 'mission villages' (reducciones) among the Guaraní, where the indigenous people lived communally, learned Catholicism and were protected from enslavement; this was key to how deeply Catholicism took root among the people of Paraguay. After the Spanish king expelled the Jesuits in 1767 the mission villages collapsed, but Catholicism had become the main faith of the Guaraní mestizo population. Although the 1992 constitution separates church and state, Catholics still make up more than eighty percent.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Evangelical, etc.)
ranking.description: Protestantism arrived in the late 19th century with European immigrants, and from the 1920s German-descended Mennonites moved from Canada and the Soviet Union into the Chaco region in the west and established autonomous colonies. In the late 20th century Pentecostal and evangelical churches expanded rapidly in cities such as Asunción and in impoverished rural areas, raising the Protestant share to about ten percent.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Paraguay is one of the most religious countries in South America, with Catholicism closely tied to family and festivals, so the non-religious make up only about 3%, mainly among educated young people in Asunción.

ranking.name: Others
ranking.description: Other religions include the traditional beliefs of a minority of indigenous people, Mormons, Jehovah's Witnesses, and the Muslim and Buddhist communities of Ciudad del Este in the east. Ciudad del Este lies at the tri-border area of Paraguay, Brazil and Argentina, and in the late 20th century attracted many Lebanese, Taiwanese and Korean merchants.

religion.background: The Guaraní originally believed in ancestral spirits and nature spirits. After Spanish colonization in the 16th century, the Guaraní mission villages established by the Jesuits in 1609–1767 rooted Catholicism deeply among the people. After independence in 1811, the dictator Francia for a time restricted the Church's power. In the 20th century immigrants such as the Mennonites brought Protestantism, and Pentecostalism has expanded in recent years. Today Catholicism is still at the core of society, and every year on 8 December more than a million believers make a pilgrimage for the feast of the Virgin of Caacupé.

language.official: The official languages are Spanish and Guaraní.

ranking.name: Bilingual Spanish and Guaraní
ranking.description: Paraguay is the only country in the Americas where most of the population speaks an indigenous language. In the colonial period Spanish men married Guaraní women, and their mixed-race descendants spoke Guaraní at home and Spanish in public affairs, making bilingualism the norm. The 1992 constitution made both official languages, and today about forty percent of the population mix the two languages in daily life; in cities 'Jopara', a mixture of the two, is common.

ranking.name: Guaraní
ranking.description: Guaraní belongs to the Tupi–Guaraní family and is the language of the indigenous people of Paraguay. The Jesuits preached in Guaraní in the mission villages, wrote grammars and printed books, making it a written language. In the Chaco War of 1932–1935, the Paraguayan army used Guaraní to transmit orders that the Bolivian army could not decipher, making it a symbol of national identity. Speakers of Guaraní alone are concentrated in rural areas and make up about one third.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Those who speak only Spanish are concentrated mainly in the upper and middle classes of cities such as Asunción. In the colonial period Spanish was the language of administration and education and has long been regarded as the language of higher social status. Urbanization and the spread of education after the 20th century have increased the proportion of urban young people who use only Spanish.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: Portuguese is mainly used by the 'Brasiguayos' (brasiguayos) in the eastern areas bordering Brazil. In the 1970s the Stroessner government opened up land in the east, attracting many Brazilian farmers to grow soybeans, greatly increasing the Portuguese-speaking population in departments such as Alto Paraná.

language.history: Guaraní is the indigenous language of Paraguay, and after Spanish colonization in the 16th century the mixed-race society formed a tradition of using Guaraní and Spanish together, with the Jesuits even publishing books in Guaraní. After the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870) in the 19th century the government for a time suppressed Guaraní and banned its use in schools. The Chaco War of 1932–1935 made Guaraní a national symbol, the 1992 constitution formally made it an official language alongside Spanish, and in 2010 a Language Law was passed to promote bilingual education.

ranking.name: Sopa paraguaya
ranking.description: A batter of cornmeal, cheese, onion, milk, eggs and lard is placed in a baking pan and baked into a soft savory corn cake, often served as a side dish for barbecued meat.
ranking.history: The name sopa paraguaya means 'Paraguayan soup', yet it is a solid cake. Legend has it that the cook of the 19th-century dictator Carlos Antonio López added too much cornmeal while making soup and had to put it in the oven, accidentally creating a delicious corn cake. Corn is the Guaraní's traditional crop, while cheese and milk come from the cattle introduced by the Spanish. It is indispensable at Christmas, weddings and family barbecues.

ranking.name: Chipa (cheese bread)
ranking.description: Dough kneaded from cassava starch, cheese, eggs and lard or butter is shaped into small rounds or rings and baked, with a crisp crust and a chewy interior and a rich cheese aroma.
ranking.history: Chipa dates from the time of the Jesuit mission villages; the Guaraní originally made bread from cassava, and after the Spanish introduced cattle, cheese and eggs were added. During Holy Week before Easter, many families bake large quantities of chipa in a traditional clay oven (tatakuá) to share with relatives and friends, since no cooking is done on Good Friday. Today it is a common breakfast sold by street vendors and on buses, eaten with yerba mate or coffee.

ranking.name: Mbejú (cassava pancake)
ranking.description: Cassava starch, cheese, milk and lard are mixed and fried in a pan into a flat round cake, crisp outside and soft and chewy inside, savory in taste, often eaten for breakfast with milk or yerba mate.
ranking.history: Mbejú is a traditional food of the Guaraní indigenous people; long before the Spanish arrived, the Guaraní made cassava starch pancakes, and the name comes from Guaraní. In the colonial period the cheese and lard brought by the Spanish were added, making it richer and more fragrant. During the War of the Triple Alliance and the Chaco War it was a convenient field ration, and today it remains a common snack at breakfast and afternoon tea.

ranking.name: Tereré (cold mate)
ranking.description: Yerba mate leaves are placed in a horn or wooden cup and steeped with ice water or fruit juice, with herbs such as mint and lemongrass added, and drunk through a metal straw, cool and thirst-quenching.
ranking.history: The Guaraní had long drunk yerba mate, and the Jesuits planted it on a large scale in the mission villages, making it a major cash crop. It is generally thought that tereré became widespread during the Chaco War of 1932–1935, when soldiers in the hot Chaco could not light fires to boil water and instead steeped it with cold water. In 2020 UNESCO inscribed the culture of tereré on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and the last Saturday of February each year is National Tereré Day.

ranking.name: Bori bori (chicken and corn dumpling soup)
ranking.description: Small dumplings kneaded from cornmeal and cheese are cooked in a broth simmered with chicken, onion, bell pepper and tomato, giving a rich, warming broth.
ranking.history: Bori bori combines the Guaraní's corn with the chicken and cheese introduced by the Spanish, and its name is generally thought to come from the Spanish 'bolita' (little ball) as pronounced in Guaraní, a microcosm of a bilingual society. It is the most popular soup in Paraguay in winter, thought to restore strength, often eaten on cold days or after illness, and is also a classic dish passed down through generations in families.
